¶1 Auzubillah Minashaitan Nirajeem

¶2 Bismillah-ir-Rahman-ir-Rahim

¶3 I hope if you remember, we mentioned different types of mysticism in the previous discussion. We have four different types of inclinations in mystical thoughts and that is mysticism of fear, mysticism of renunciation, mysticism of love and mysticism of Gnosis, which is knowledge and maarifah. We discussed about the three types of mysticism and their main proponents and Sufis who followed each attitude, fear, law and love. Now just quickly look at those mystics who were following mysticism of maarifah meaning that they placed more emphasis on knowledge than love or renunciation. One Sufi I will only mention here because there are many, many different Sufis and mystics here that if you want to pay attention to them, it will take a long time.

¶4 Only the most prominent people in this field is Al Hakim Al Tirmidhi. Of course it is different from the term of Sahih Al-Tirmidhi. He was a Mystic of the 3rd century and since he was Hakim means he was philosopher as well. So he was a Mystic philosopher and that's why he brought this idea of gnostic emphasis in mysticism rather than just emphasizing on renunciation and love. So his surname Al Hakim or his actually nickname or laqab Al Hakim means the philosopher points to the fact that through him some Hellenistic philosophical ideas penetrated into Sufism as we have it today as well. We have lots of new platonic ideas in our theoretical mysticism which have come through these people who are Sufis and the philosophers and were acquainted to lots of hedonistic philosophical ideas especially Plato.

¶5 Plato and Pluto both of them play a great role in shaping the theoretical outlook of the Islamic mysticism of course and Tirmidhi’s main contribution to the mystical theory is probably his seal of the saints Khatm al Awliya which of course then this topic of Khatm al Awliya which was mentioned very roughly by Tirmidhi was taken on later on very elaborately by Ibne Arabic. And he said as we have Khatm al Ambiya, we have Khatm al Awliya as well. However he didn't regard say for example Imam Al Asr as Khatm al Awliya or Khatm al Awsiya. He said that there is a khatm to the whole knowledge of mystics and he regarded himself to be Khatm al Awliya somehow maybe it was some sort of illusion or whatever.

¶6 We cannot judge what he meant by this. But this seal of the Saints, when he talked about this then he started to mention the idea that was very familiar to us today that is quds or the pivot or the pillar of the mystic knowledge that should exist at every age, you know the Sufis in every tariqa they have a quds. Quds is a pole, a pole to which everyone should rely and to which everyone should turn. These ideas came very early in the 3^(rd) century of mysticism and it was mentioned in this book “Seal of the Saints” by Hakim Al Tarmidhi. So he was the leader of the Sufi hierarchy. According to him the same governs the universe.

¶7 Now again something which is very close to Shia idea of the power of immah that they have Wilayatu-e-Takvini. Wilayatu-e-Takvini meaning that they have power over the world of creation. Not only power over the world of Tashri or Alaamut Tashri or Wilayatut Tashri. Not only in the world of religion, they have power in this. Now, of course some of the ideas of Shia are influenced by the extremist views which were mentioned in this thing by this Sunnis. It's amazing that they thought about the saints in a way that we even don’t think about our imam. They said that the Saint is actually the vicegerent of Allah and the host and he can do whatever he wants.

¶8 The whole universe is under his console. He is our level Akbar and the universe is Alaamul Akbar or vice versa, depending how they actually interpreted these two terms. The bigger world is the saint and the smaller world is the universe and it's all under his control. All these ideas you can see very early in mystical thought. So according to him the saint govern the universe. Certain groups of 374 or 300 saints are entrusted with value duties in maintaining the world order. It still exists. They say there is a ghaus and then there are autaad which are the pillars of the earth. Three or seven he mentioned. Then there are abdaal which are 40 or 300, which again they control everything in this world, and if they do not exist, the world will perish.

¶9 The same ideas that we have about Imams, but they take it to very extreme type of concept which is not even acceptable by Shia. They were influenced by the Shia, they took it into very extreme and then when we want to bring them back into the Shia world, we see that these ideas are very extreme. Even we do not regard some of these things for our Aimmah or for the Prophet. Now, of course, this is mysticism which is philosophy which has been very close to a type of philosophical ideology. Also, like the prophets who see if Muhammad, the saints also have their own saints and different saints thought of themselves to be the saint of all the saints.

¶10 The decrees of saint Hakim Tirmidhi are related to the degrees of illumination and Gnosis preached by the Sufi. It is not the hierarchy of love. Now, this is very important, because in the mysticism of love, the more love you have, the nearer you are, the closer you are to Allah. Here, the more knowledge you have of Allah, the closer you are to the realm of Allah. Now, some people have tried to actually make a compromise between these two views saying that where does love come from? It comes from maarifah. The more you know God, the more you feel love for him, the more you're away from him, the more ignorant of God you are less love, you see or you do not see any love at all.

¶11 So love is the outcome of maarifah and therefore these two schools of mysticism of love and maarifah can come close to each other in this way. Also there is emphasis on Gnosis, maarifah. The term agnostic comes from this as well because gnosis and agnosis is the opposite of maarifah for those people who say we have no knowledge about God. We cannot find any knowledge about god. This was something which came right from the beginning of the discussions about God in philosophy and mysticism, prepares the way for later philosophical speculation. If you remember at the beginning of our talk, we said that mystics somehow distinguish two types of knowledge, maarifah and ilm. And they say maarifah is knowledge of god and ilm is the knowledge of the universe.

¶12 And with two different methods, maarifah is gained through purification and ilm is gained through study and experience. Now, of course, this, as I said, is not a Quranic type of terminology. It's something which has come from Sufis as the origin comes from Hakim Al Tirmidhi which actually distinguishes these two types of knowledge. Yeah, I think that's all I wanted to say about Hakim Al Tirmidhi, he was very important. I mentioned him because he was actually a turning point in bringing a type of theorization into mystical souls which existed. The influence of which existed for a long time and many of the ideas of Ibne Arabi which is the culmination of mystical civilization have come from Hakim Al Tirmidhi as well as others, of course.

¶13 Now we have two great mystics of two different types of mysticism I want to discuss here because you might come across these two names very much. These are most famous mystics of the third century. And mystics of two different type of mysticism which have left its imprint on the future development of all mysticism as well. Abu Yazid al Bistami also known as Bayazid Bastami which is more easy way of pronunciation and Junayd al Baghdadi who is the culmination of the mysticism in the first century, after which, of course, mysticism took a different path. Now, they represent two different types of mysticism, mysticism of intoxication and mysticism of sovereignty or sukr. And now some mystics they were inclined to go into a world that they could lose them, they couldn't see anything but God and they just talk and speak of him rather than themselves.

¶14 They wanted to somehow lose themselves in God and become intoxicated with this pleasant feeling of being annihilated in God. This is called mysticism of intoxication. And in lots of Persian poetry, of course, I don't know whether you have it in your own language, they talk about musty intoxication, that you reach intoxication when you leave all the bonds and attachments that you have in this world. And then you have that feeling, nice feeling of forgetting everything, but of course, here for Allah. Now, of course many mystics like Junayd say that this is only a trinity experience of God that you will have. Of course, you will see the great mystics which are very often mentioned in different books and are commended because we human beings are inclined towards intoxication; we like to lose everything, and to only have the feeling of God.

¶15 That's why the mystics should present this school of intoxication, I'm sure one of them you have had very much Mansoor Hallaj. I'm sure all of you have heard of him, who was of course, executed because of his very unacceptable statements that he made about his own self and his relation to God. He was one of those who was intoxicated by this experience of God and usually he has become the role model of all those who are somehow feeling that they want to go towards Allah lose everything and sacrifice everything, offer everything for Allah. However, as we will see, the mystics like Junayd and people of course more advanced in mysticism regard these as children, regard as in these people to be just limiting mystics who have lost themselves at the beginning steps of mystical experience.

¶16 Now let's look at both these of course Bayazid and Junayd, the representative of these two schools. Abu Yazid, he was born in Bastam, a small city in the north of Iran. I don't think you can hear me mystic coming from any place other than Iran. Iran was a hotbed of these mystical experiences and he formulated the experience of fanah of course we discussed it and still is a great concept in mysticism and annihilation. For the first time he spoke of this you see, middle of the third century and end of the second century, this concept of annihilation and fannah came into the Islamic mystical thoughts. And he was asked about renunciation. Now this is very interesting.

¶17 He was asked what is zuhd? We have that mysticism of zuhd and renunciation. He said, renunciation has no value because I am after intoxication, nothing else. I was three days in renunciation on the fourth day I have finished. Now look how interesting is his speech. The first day, I renounced this world, the second day, I renounced the other world. The third day, I denounced everything save god. No, of course, these statements have no meaning for us because we don't have those experiences that these people have in their inner soul. What's the meaning of renouncing the other world meaning that they are not buying, they are not desiring anything but Allah. Just it reminds me the statement of Imam Sajjad (as) in Sahifa-e-Sajjadiya, “Oh, God, if I had the capacity to be burnt into your hell, if I had that power and energy, I would have asked you to burn in hellfire, because I deserve it.

¶18 But I don't have that capacity. So what should I do? And this is exactly the same thing, renouncing even the other world and thinking only about Allah. So he says, on the second day I renounced the other world, the third day I renounce everything save God. When the fourth day came, nothing was left to me but God. I reached a desperate bonding and I heard the voice, “you are not strong enough to endure with me alone”. I said, that is exactly what I want. Then the voice said, “you have found you have found”. Now this loneliness of deserting everything, everything that we have some sort of attachment to the soul, anything that we come out of our desires of course, is something that not everyone can indure.

¶19 So this is how he described his own attitude towards zuhd. There are famous statements which are made by Sufis when they are intoxicated, they go they lose control and they only say things that they experienced but it doesn't make sense for us. It is sometimes translated as theo pathetic statement something which states about God which are not right of course, which are unhealthy, but it comes out of those instances which these mystics were in type of excitement and ecstasy. Shath are the famous statement of Sufis when they are intoxicated. So his famous statement fascinated many mystics after he said, “Praise is to me, how great my majesty is”. Now, of course, what this means is that I am God, isn't it?

¶20 Praise is to me, how great my majesty is. How great I am. He is still trying to explain this very much, because this is very famous from Bayazid. And some of them have said that this is when Bayazid completely lost control and Allah was speaking from his tongue. And in fact, the same way as Allah was speaking from that tree of Prophet Musa. “Inneee Anal laah” 28:30 the tree was saying that, I am the Lord. And we know that the tree was not Allah. Allah was speaking from the tree. The best explanation which somehow exonerates these Sufis from saying funny things is that he came to a situation that Allah was speaking from his tongue.

¶21 Now, however, this is not acceptable by many of those mystics, who had the same experiences. They say that no, he came to a position that he loves himself. And he could not see himself. He only could see God and he saw himself unified with God. And therefore, when he looked at himself, he didn't see himself he saw God and then he said, “Praise is to me, how great my majesty is”. However, the difference between the two explanations is that, you come to a station you come to status with Allah will speak from your tongue or you speak when you see the glory of Allah while you have been removed out of the way, there is no you anymore.

¶22 This is the best way that we can explain these types of sathiyat or serious statements made by Sufis. Now by this practice, mortification and emptying himself up himself until he has reached at least for a moment, the world of absolute unity.

¶23 Of course, this unity with God is not accepted by later Sufis, this is something they say this is a wrong interpretation of the experiences of the Sufis where it said that the lover, beloved, and love are one. Of course, Attar was very much influenced by Bayazid as well because this Mantiq al-tayr, the Conference of the Birds, I don't know, if anyone has read this book, Conference of the Birds is translation of Mantiq al-tayr by Attar. He actually believes very much that you come to a station that the lover, the beloved, and the love are the same thing you cannot differentiate between them. What he says in this book is very interesting for anyone who wants to read it, it says that once the birds came together and they had a conference that they want to find the biggest bird in this world, Simorgh.

¶24 Now, Simorgh is a Persian word. It is a type of mythical bird which dos not exists, but is the representation of the glory of the birds or something like that. Now, they wanted to go and find the Simorgh. However, of course, many of them disagree that no, this is a long journey, we don't want to go and all these issues. And at the end, some of them agreed and they started their journey. They came through several different big tests and hurdles. And at any place, they started to argue with each other, some of them returned, some of them died, some of them went forward. Now, at the end of all these, only 30 birds remained that came to the place where Simorgh was living.

¶25 They came to the search of Simorgh, they came to the place and they didn't find anything. And it was amazing that after all those toils and troubles and problems. In the end, the birds learn that they themselves are the Simorgh; the name “Simorgh” in Persian means thirty (si) birds (morgh) and they found out that Simorgh was themselves. They were looking for something which was existing in themselves. This is exactly what Bayazid and mystic were teaching that the lover, the beloved and love are one thing. You just have to unify with this. Now, also, of course, this comes into this mysticism of intoxication. Junayd, the leader of Baghdadi School was his student. Of course, the student was bigger than the teacher.

¶26 Although he believed that Bayazid did not reach the final goal of the seeker because as I said, they regarded this type of intoxication at the beginning of the world. There were lots of other stations that they had to follow. Al-Hallaj believed that Bayazid had arrived only at the threshold of the Divine. And he was so intoxicated so excited that he couldn't move further. And many people say the same thing about Al-Hallaj himself that he had just under threshold of divine and he didn't move forward. His name occurred in paucity more than that of any other mystic, Bayazid with the exception of course Al-Hallaj which everyone has heard about. Now Junayd Al Baghdadi of course is a completely different Sufi.

¶27 So he is the one you remember we had said Sufis had several journeys and at the end of the first journey they come to annihilation and then they have to start the second journey which brings for them baqah after fanah existence another annihilation. This is what actually Junayd found. He moved further than that intoxicated ecstasy of the mystics. Okay, like many other mystics, he came from Iran. As I said, all these mystics came from Iran. And, of course, he went and lived in Baghdad and that's why he was called Junayd Al-Baghdadi. He was born in Nahavand which is very close to my birthplace, Kermanshah and then settled in Baghdad. And he was educated by his maternal uncle, Sari al-Saqati, who was a great mystic himself.

¶28 I didn't mention his name, because if I mention all these people you would have got confused. He was a disciple of Al-Muhasibi about whom we of course, spoke in details. And then he is regarded as a Sultan and the urafa calls him Sayyid at-Taifa. Like for example, the jurist calls him Shaikh at-Taifa whilst the urafa calls him Sayyid at-Taifa. He was the biggest among the Sufis. And he emphasized understate of sovereignty, as we mentioned, as contrasted by intoxication. Bayazid preferred mystical intoxication because it obliterates the human attributes and annihilation is completely gone. However, of course, Junayd considered the second sovereignty the highest and the preferred state. According to him, after the attitude of intoxication man becomes more aware of himself in the life in God when all these attributes have posturized.

¶29 Now, why is this difference come because of course, Bayazid moved towards Allah and stopped at one place and Junayd was the first one probably that moved more further ahead and found that after this annihilation there is something else to see. It's just like for example, you set on a journey to explore what's on the way and you go, say several 1000 kilometres and you say yes, at the end of this journey there is a river and everyone thinks that at the at the end of the world, there is a river. However, there are better equipment more powerful people and they can go further ahead, they can say no beyond the river there are many, many other things you haven't seen because what was the situation with Junayd Al Baghdadi of course, and according to Junayd annihilation is not the ultimate goal but baqah or remaining of which we talked of course in detail is a new life in God.

¶30 He was critic of Al-Hallaj who spoke openly about mystical experience and develops a set language of allusion (isharah) which speaks about the subjects that makes it unintelligible for the outsiders. And this became a type of custom among old mystics. They speak in a language that other people cannot understand. They understand only themselves. Yes, because then they become like Allah. I mean, they say things which are very funny. If they reveal their experiences ordinary people cannot tolerate it. I don't know whether you have heard this hades that, if Abuzar knew what is in the heart of Salman he would have said he's a kafir. Okay. Why because the status of Salman was very high in terms of knowledge.

¶31 And he knew things about God that if he had revealed it had he revealed it, people would have said that he's a kafir because ordinarily people have a concept about God, which cannot digest the various stages and understand and experiences. And usually mystics say that we have this poem of Hafiz, you know why our friend Al-Hallaj was under barrels because he revealed the secret. And that was what he deserved. He shouldn't reveal the secret of this. Of course, this is very natural, because the limit of people understands about God is, is very low, their understanding is very limited. And if you could tell them something which they cannot understand, digest and analyse and of course, they cannot accept that completely.

¶32 It's just like confusing a child. I mean, why is it meaning these secrets are not allowed? It's just like, if you want to confuse the child about God, it's not good. You shouldn't confuse the child. And these mystics shouldn't confuse us about God. Of course, they have high knowledge but why should they confuse us? You don't understand it even if they say, so what's the point of saying. This is why of course, Junayd was very much against Al-Hallaj saying all those sorts of things and he says that he deserves to be denounced because it revealed the secrets. Junayd died in 298. He existed. He was born towards the end of the era of Aimmah. So he's his main fruitful life was after the ghaybah of Imam-Asr.

¶33 Okay, just one more mystic we want to explore. We come down to a later time Ash-Shaykh al-Akbar Muhyiddin Arabi. Well, it's very difficult to talk about Muhyiddin Arabi because he's voluminous type of work on mysticism is very confusing first of all. Secondly, he has become the Shaykh al-Akbar for both Shia & Sunni mystics and they regard him as the culmination of the theoretical mysticism and experiences and he claims many different things are very, very, very difficult to accept. He claims experiences which are difficult to think that a human being could have had such experiences. And just then quickly, I touched upon some aspects of his life. And so he was Muhyiddin on the order of Shaykh Abd al-Qadir Jilani.

¶34 Shaykh Abd al-Qadir Jilani is the author or the head of the Jilaniya tariqa which is of course, a very powerful and important tariqa and this Shaykh Abd al-Qadir Jilani he himself was a great mystic. We will discuss about when we come to Sufi Tariqa Inshallah. When he saw Muhyiddin when he was a child, he somehow found very, very powerful type of understanding of the other world in him and therefore he called him Muhyiddin told father to look after him very carefully. Muhyiddin means the one who revives the religion of course. And although in his autograph notes usually signed as Abu Abdullah, of course, for those who read his books. Everyday miracles, at the age of 12 the great Shaykh narrates what took place.

¶35 Now this is a very interesting, I have noticed, although it's not a great miracle, but I have brought this to mention because sometimes we do things that does have some sort of effects and only what if you could see aalamul barzakh, we could see the effects of these issues. He says that one day I fell seriously ill and went into a coma. So serious and everyone's thought I’m dead. And then I saw in my vision some horrible looking people who are seeking to hurt me. I noticed the person pulled out grace and strength breathing out a wonderful perfume which defended me against them and threw them away. Who are you? I asked. And this they replied, I am Surah Yaseen.

¶36 I am your protector, then I regained consciousness to find my father, may God have mercy on him at my bedside in tears and he had just finished reciting Surah Yaseen. Now, of course, this young boy was he was 12. In that coma situation, seeing that, of course, he's did not know that his father was reciting Surah Yaseen for his cure. And just seeing in that aalamul barzakh that someone is coming, very powerful, very centred type of driving away all those horrible creatures and then he's saying, I'm Surah Yaseen. He tells us that he was very much connected to aalamul barzakh and vice versa and the type of images which are formed. If you remember, we said anything that we do here has an image in aalamul barzakh.

¶37 And this is very much, of course, approved by lots of rivayat and also by the Quran that these images are formed although we do not see. We think that is just words, we say, for example, if we tell a lie, or we if we start to console, a person, it's just words that you utter. However, these have a shape an image in the world of barzakh according to how they are formed. And those images are real things, as he has seen that this Surah Yaseen was a real man coming to protect him. And, of course, the things that Muhyiddin mentioned in his books show this very much that during the whole life, his writing was completely moving from this world to barzakh and coming back.

¶38 He says that I've seen all the prophets, for example, and certainly the prophets living in barzakh. He said that, for example, I saw the Prophet, he gave me a book and told me that write this book, and this is full of hikmah or something like this, we'll come to this later on, and he was moving. So, no wonder why he was became such a great mystic. He had a type of disposition, which gave him the power to have these experiences and thinking. Certainly, we cannot have those experiences because we are not so much constituted in the same way to freely move to the world of barzakh and come. Of course, we are different, you see, some people see very fine dreams, which come true very, very soon, very quickly and some people never see dreams at all.

¶39 This is because some are more connected to aalamul barzakh and some are less connected. It is not a merit that we are going to be rewarded for because it's something which is part of our nature. However, those who are more connected could more easily experience things than other people who have difficulty. For Ibne Arabi the way he had introduced himself and the way he has cured all these issues and no one else has been able to prove on what he said. It shows that he had that sort of disposition and constitution which was different from others. Inspiration, Ibne Arabi claims that he wrote through inspiration. He usually writes that I do not write on my own accord.

¶40 These are what I am inspired to write. And that's why he had lost of enemies. Even in Iran now, you can see that he's the most loved among some and the most hated amongst some because of his claim are totally unbelievable for some people. He authored many great books which according to him originates from divine inspiration, the mystical experiences he went through in life, where his inspirations write ups, an attempt to explain this to me. And it's very interesting that you said whatever I say, and whatever I'm inspired, are just understandings from the verses of the Quran and I have nothing beyond. It's all an understanding that Allah has given to me that I understand different things.

¶41 And I experience the tahweel of all these verses maybe. He his voluminous book “Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya” his Meccan illuminations while he was in Makah. Usually the mystics call the highest experiences of the supernatural to have the opening of the heart or the victories or the illumination, anything like that. Now, it is an encyclopaedic work founded on the Quran and discussion of Islamic wisdom viewed from the perspective of the stages of the mystic part. However, he mentioned that, I mean, the stories he mentioned in this are amazing. He was given many parts of this book from different prophets, for example and of course, many people have relied on them because they have found them somehow, similar to their experiences.

¶42 All these issues about asmaullah, the names of Allah, the attributes of Allah and the experience of Allah have originated from Ibne Arabi. Of course, we have in hades of aimmah, but no one no one had experienced and had theorizes. I was reading a book by Allahma Tabatabai about asmaullah. I was so amazed that how this man has this knowledge about asmaullah and how has he analysed this. Then I read Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya by Ibne Arab. I saw that he had taken all those from Ibne Arabi. And, of course, he didn’t say that I have originated because Allahma Tabatabi was very much fond of Ibne Arabi and he was completely emphasizing everywhere that all these knowledge has come from Ibne Arabi.

¶43 And even Hasan Zadeh Amuli, he mentions that Allahma Tabatabai was saying that all these I have learned from Ibne Arabi. Now, I mentioned this, because what he says about Ibne Arabi is so unbelievable, that you cannot think that someone like Allahma Tabatabai would say that I have gained knowledge from Ibne Arabi. However, the experiences that Allahma Tabatabai had matched very much with whatever Ibne Arabi had experienced. And it's amazing and it's not for us to judge because it needs someone who has the experience and then goes to the book and see how they have theorized. And also he has Fusus al-Hikam, The Bezels of Wisdom. This he says he received directly from the Prophet Mohammed who appeared to him in Damascus in a dream and he told him, this is the book to be taken to the people.

¶44 And he woke up and then he found out that he had the knowledge of his book in his heart. And he started to write the book. Of course, the book, if you read it, you don't understand anything from this just a secret language in a way that only the mystics can understand or those have some of these experiences and have previous knowledge about it. However, he says that, I have received it directly from the Prophet; he gave me the book in dreams. I woke up and had the whole book in my heart and I wrote it up and that it is possible. Now he has also more than 800 books. Now you can see how, of course he was very busy with his followers, his journeys and it's amazing how he found all this time to write all these books.

¶45 And of course, Usman Bin Yahya has listed his bibliography in two big volumes in French. Of course, you can imagine two big volumes of books of only one person, how huge he has worked on. One of his works is an interpretation of the Quran in 90 volumes, of course not published. It is just mentioned although we cannot find it now at the moment. He influenced many, many mystics after himself and especially the type of mysticism that we have in Iran today is very much influenced by an Ibne Arabi. As I said, Allahma Tabatabi, Ayatullah Hassanzadeh and their teachers were all influenced by this school of Ibne Arabi. Some of the greatest characters known to us were influenced by Ibne Arabi was Jalal al-Din Muḥammad Rumi.

¶46 He was the author of Masnavi who was connected to Ibne Arabi via Sadruddin al-Qunawi who was a disciple of the latter and friend and close associate of the other. Ala al-Dawlah Simnani, he was a formidable mystic of the seventh century who criticized Ibne Arabi. He also admits he was greatly influenced by him and Shaykh Mohammad Lahiji founder of Nurbakhshī Sufi order, and many others, many, many others were influenced by Ibne Arabi. Shah Ni’matullah Wali (founder of the Ni’matullahī Sufi order) were both deeply influenced by ibn ‘Arabi and these influences are not limited to Sufi sheikhs and orders. He also includes great Shiite Gnostics such as Sayyid Haydar Âmulli; who wrote a commentary and work based on ibn ‘Arabi’s theoretical ‘Irfan and also the whole bunch of contemporary Shiite mystics.

¶47 And not only that, he influenced Shia philosophers like Mulla Sadra (Sadruddin-as-Shirazi) and actually Shirazi says that he tackled the Mutaaliya is a rationalized way of the theoretical irfan of Ibne Arabi. Was Ibne Arabi Shia or Sunni? It is difficult to say that he was a Shia. And if you say he is a Sunni, he had his own experiences of reality. And he had great respect for aimmah and Abu Bakr and Omar as was well. So it's very confusing, very perplexing and it seems that these realities could not be found by mystical experience. Mystical experience is only about the World of God and about the world of human beings and what they do in this world.

¶48 It is very, very dodgy somehow, you cannot say that a person is very mystical has lots of miracles, lots of qaramat and if he is a Shia then Shia faith is right and if he is a Sunni then Sunni faith is right. It's not possible to say that. This Shia Sunni business should only be solved by rational arguments rather than by experiences. And amazingly those critics of Ibne Arabi say that, why Shia mystics follow Ibne Arabi? Why, for example, in one of his statements in Futuhat, he says that there are some group of people who are called Rajabiyun, who fast all in the month of Rajab and they are the people who are described by the prophet as those who receive the blessings of Rajab and they say that I met some of these Rajabiyun and some of them explain for me they saw Shias in form of pigs.

¶49 Of course, this is very irritating and we have some mystics in Mashad. The last time we went there we saw one ulema, who was a critic of Ibne Arabi and critic Allama Tabatabi and critic of Hassanzadeh Amuli that why do you follow Ibne Arabi? He says that Rajabiyun Shia in the form of pigs and why do you say that Ibne Arabi was a Shia or was respectable? Now okay how can we can explain this? That maybe those Shias were sinful Shias. It was not because they were Shias that they saw them in the form of pigs but because they were sinful people. He had great respect for Ahlul Bayt and Imam Asr as well. He believed in Imam Ali but of course, people say he only talks about khatamul Awliya and Khatamul Awsiya but he's talking more about himself than others.

¶50 Sometimes his statements are very confusing. And that's why people are left in this status of not knowing what really the idea of Ibne Arabi about wilayah because the topic of wilayah is very important in mysticism. But they see the wilayah not only as wilayah of aimmah, they see the wilayah as wilayah-e-zuhd, wilayah of mystics as well. So, I don't know, it's, it's very difficult to judge. What I'm, I'm trying to say is that his experiences and the way he theorizes match with experiences of many others mystics and they found no better language than the language of Ibne Arabi to explain it. And therefore, they are very much fond of using statements of Ibne Arabi other than any other mystics despite of course it’s an insult to some Shia idea for example or despite some of the arguments that Sunnis would not accept, very much attack on Ibne Taymiyyah for claiming that he was held for destroying the religion or something like that.

¶51 And they said that he was influenced by Shia for example. Many of his ideas that he was saying, is difficult to judge such situations. Now as well as influencing the Isma’īli Shi’ites, who chiefly refer to the Qur’anic commentary of ibn ‘Arabi. He played a pivotal role in the school of hikmah without which great personalities would never have the opportunity to become what they have. Personalities such as Mulla Sadra, as I mentioned, all his Hikamtul Mutaliya is something which is actually rationalization of his mystical theories. Mulla Ali Nuri, Mullâ Hadi Subziwari, the great Shia of course philosopher and Imam Khomeini of course, one of the things he mentioned to Gorbachev is that, why don't you let people your people in Russia go and know about Ibne Arabi and know the true face of Islam and the reality of religion.

¶52 Now, of course, after he wrote that letter to Gorbachev, lots of articles were going around criticizing Ibne Arabi and then criticizing Imam Khomeini. Why Imam Khomeini talks about Ibne Arabi and why he says that Gorbachev should encourage people to go and read Ibne Arabi’s Book. You read examples that he mentioned, for example, he said things about Abu Bakr and Omar. He says that once I had a vision, I saw Abu Bakr at the right hand of Allah and Omar at the left hand and Ali sitting down lower than them, of course, is against Shia thoughts but this is how he says. How can we explain it? What you saw was wrong. As I said, you cannot 100% accept someone or reject.

¶53 Certainly he had something valuable in what he wrote. However, when it comes to Shia, of course the Shia will say, well, of course, the visions because the vision you construe in your mind according to what you already know, according to your theology and what you saw might not have been in the same order as you saw. It just was created due to the type of theology in which you believe. So now it is and is the way it has been. Now the controversies although he was considered a great personality by many scholars to the extent that they called him Al Waliyul Kaamil (the Perfect Saint) and Qutb al-Aqtab (the Pole of Poles). He also had his opponents who refer to him as Mumit al-Dīn (the Killer of the Faith) instead of being the reviver of the faith and call him Mahi al-Dīn (the Effacer of the Faith) and all these are written in different philosophical books.

¶54 Last time I talked about two very interesting books. I hope I remember the names because the names are very interesting. One two volume book was written by one of the students of Allahma Tabatabi. Al Kalaamul Mateen Fi Tasshayyo Muhyuddin. He posted a powerful statement in the tasshayyo of Ibne Arabi and he had filed in 2 volumes to prove that Ibne Arabi was Shia and not a Sunni. And then I saw another book which what it was something like this, but it was the final word in that Ibne Arabi was a very prejudice Sunni and I find it interesting. Both of them have actually provided arguments that the work from different parts of Ibne Arab’s book showed that he was a Shia, the other parts showed that he was a Sunni.

¶55 And of course the one which was we shouldn't be unjust the one who had mentioned that he was a Sunni, his argument was much much more powerful than the other one, the other one was a very weak. Anyhow, this is how it is. And now, one thing of course, of Ibne Arabi has remained to discuss which are a bit hesitant to discuss it or not, the theory of Wahdat ul Wujud. Wahdatul Wujood, you know this has come from Ibne Arabi and he had theorized this. Others had of course, some sort of shakhiyat about it theosophical statements or some sorts of allusions to it, but they could not feel like it very well as Ibne Arabi had theorized it.

¶56 Now just a glance, okay. The theory Wahdat ul Wujud, we have different opinions about the existence. Now just I mentioned what are those differences? And then we will see what Wahdat ul Wujud mean. One theory is Qasratul Wujud wal Mawjud, diversity of the existence and the existence. Usually peripatetic philosophers, machine philosophers they believe in this that you have all types of beings who have god as you have the universe as you have the sun as you have the earth as you have animals, all these are separate beings. Allah is a separate thing, these things are separate beings as well. However, this is very difficult to understand how one being can be actually outside the realm of us.

¶57 Is there anything there outside? So this was the main idea of my machine philosophers there are lots of wujudaat and lots of mujudaat. Mujudaat have their own wujud. Different beings have their own existence their own separate existence, this is one thing. The other was that unity of the existence and diversity of their existence. Existence means mujud, existence means mujud. What it means? There is one existence and all other beings are mahiyyat. They are just beings of course, which take their existence from that one big existence Okay. Attributed to the existence is possible according to essential of Mahiyyat. Now we don't go into this. This is what Shaqiyoon, the illuminatious philosophers have actually proposed. What is the difference between this one and the previous one?

¶58 In this one, you say that there is one existence. There's only one existence in this world, and that's God Okay. However, there are different mahiyyat which take their existence from that one existence. In the previous one, Qasratul Wujud wal Mawjud you didn't have one big existence and then everything else gaining their existence from that one, everyone had their own independent existence. However, God had one big existence and had created other existences. In the second theory there is no other existence. There are existences which have their existence taken from that one big existence. In the first theory, there is one big existence, an existence which actually causes other existences to come. They are different, independent. Okay, this is another theory about the diversity and unity of existence.

¶59 The third one Wahdat ul Wujud wal Mujud, unity of the existence and diversity of the existent; this is Mulla Sadra’s and all Persian philosophers before Islam Pahlaviyyun. Actuallu Mulla Sadra draws philosophical ideas of Persain hikmah very much because they will also probably be influenced by Platonic ideas. So, he says there is one wujud and there is one mujud and not different mujudaat. There is only one mujud. There is only one existence, although that existence is uique however it has ranks from strong to weak. Pahlaviyyun, the Old Persian philosophers they had this parable of synchronizing the existence god and the creation to light. They said we have we have a big light like the light of sun and a small lightbut all of them are light.

¶60 It's just one existence however the light has different levels of strength and enormity. So, we have the very strong one, the weak one but it is all one light. There is one light that has been graded and these come to some limitations which I will explain later on. And the first theory, Unity of existence, the theory of the mystics of course of Ibne Arabi there is only the existence and all the existence beings are but different manifestations and states and the specification. It is very difficult to understand what it means. But I want to ask you a question; I want you to think it. When God created, where is that creation? Is that outside god or is it a new existence that previous did not take this?

¶61 It is god or it is something in addition to god or is something which is already there. Which one? It existed in the eternal world but where is it in the world of existence? What brings about? What comes about? What is it the god brings about? Is it something outside him, separate from him? So we are independent existence beings or different type of existence. We are just like a type of manifestation of what is in the world of god which has shown itself in this way. This is almost what actually the theory of .. says. It states that you cannot say that there's anything besides god. Of course you cannot say that this is different from platonic theory because platonic theory says that God is subtotal of whatever exists in the universe.

¶62 So if you put all the creation together it stops because it will be the end of the cycle. However this is completely different from this theory. And this is why Ibne Arabi says that whatever you see, is god, is not god. It’s different than god. It doesn't mean that of course we do not exist at all. The mystics say that you cannot understand this theory of Wahdat ul Wujud wal Mujud except through experience. If you don't have mystical experiences you cannot, it’s very difficult to understand this. Mulla Sadra wanted to come close to Wahdat ul Wujud wal Mujud and rationalise but it was very difficult to rationalise. So he came very close to it by this theory of tashqeeq, different rank of existence, so the dependent aspects of one big existence.

¶63 Now they say that how the creation comes about? They say that Allah is the eternal creator who created some sort of beings which did not exist at all. It was just unplanned or some imagination, okay. These beings have their own limits. Some of them were like human beings and angels and quite organised type of world but it did not exist or just some sort of something between being and not being. Then of course, he gave them existence from that eternal existence that he have. So when we look at these when we look me, certainly I’m not god or a part of god because those limitations which were at the beginning eternally planned by Allah. I have come to existence doe to my relation to him or due to that existence relationship.

¶64 I have gained existence from him and that’s the meaning of “la hawla wala quwwata illa billah” meaning that here is no power and no strength except with Allah. It is non-understandable at all. It is only understandable for those who come to such an experience like Al-Hallaj or Bayazid. They say there's nothing but god. They will come to that state and will see that there is nothing but god. It is all just limitation, manifestation, specifications that Allah has given to that weak existence. And Imam Ali says he is with everything but doesn’t need anything. He is different from everything but not away from anything. And this paradoxical thing “Huwa Al-Awwalu Wa Al-Akhiru Wa Az-Zahiru Wa Al-Batinu” he is manifest and he is the hidden.

¶65 You see His manifestation but he's not him. He is completely hidden. This is not understood but with experiences and this is what actually Ibne Arabi gave to the world of mysticism, a true relationship of God with his creation. It was not theorized as such. He theorised it saying very clearly. It was there, yes. It was in the Quran Wa Az-Zahiru Wa Al-Batinu, this is of course. Well we say what is in the Quran means that it is Wahdat ul Wujud of course before that people did not say that it was Wahdat ul Wujud. They didn’t understand it in this way. It was Ibne Arabi who actually theorised in this way. I made translation of that statement of Nahjul Balagha.

¶66 It was there as a statement but not found as a theory. They couldn’t actually explain. After Ibne Arabi explained in the light of this theory of Wahdat ul Wujud very clearly, they said this is actually referring to what Ibne Arabi mentioned in his theory of Wahdat ul Wujud. It is not illusion. It is more real than you think. Its real but it is a manifestation of Allah and this manifestation is very real. It is not illusion. However it is not separate from god but still it is not god. It is very difficult to understand. Our mind cannot understand because it is not set to understand. It is only through hard experience that it can be understood.

¶67 And this is what Ibne Arabi says. He says you can never rationalise this theory. It is above the rank of reason. You cannot by reason grasp this. It is something only that you can experience. Even human beings who‘s soul can be a reflection of the attributes of Allah still are the same or different? We cannot say that they are same or different. You have to grasp something in middle which could not be understood by reasoning but something that can only be experienced.

¶68 Wa sallahu ala mohammadin wa aale hittahereen.
